lead: A petrol engine needs a spark at the right plug at the right moment. Battery-coil ignition stores energy in a coil's magnetic field and releases it as a high-voltage pulse when a contact breaker opens. Magneto ignition does the same job but generates its own current from a rotating magnet, so it needs no battery. Both systems appear on small engines, older cars and motorcycles, and aircraft piston engines; electronic ignition now replaces the contact breaker in most new cars.
prereq: You need: the SI engine cycle from Unit 1 and the sensor-ECU idea from 2.5.

blocks.text: The battery supplies 12 V direct current. The ignition switch connects it to the primary winding, a few hundred turns of thick copper wire. Current rises and builds a magnetic field in the iron core. The contact breaker is a pair of points opened by a cam on the distributor shaft, which turns at half crank speed on a four-stroke engine; the points stay closed while the field builds. A small condenser sits across the breaker points.

When the breaker opens, primary current falls quickly. The magnetic field collapses. The changing field links the secondary winding, about a hundred times as many turns of fine wire on the same core. Mutual induction produces a high voltage, often 15 kV to 30 kV, enough to jump the spark plug gap. The condenser limits arcing at the points and helps the field collapse faster.

The distributor is a rotary switch. It sends the secondary voltage to the plug of the cylinder ready to fire, in the engine's firing order. The spark then ignites the compressed mixture. Some syllabi call battery-coil ignition coil ignition.

blocks.where: E is the energy stored in the primary magnetic field (J); L is the primary inductance (H); I is the primary current (A) when the breaker opens.

sections.h3: Magneto ignition: making its own current

blocks.text: A magneto generates its own primary current. In the common rotating-magnet type, a permanent magnet on a shaft driven by the engine turns past a fixed core that carries the primary and secondary windings; in the older rotating-armature type the windings turn between fixed magnets. Either way the flux through the primary changes and induces a current. The contact breaker interrupts it at the firing point, and the secondary produces the high-voltage spark. A condenser across the breaker works as in battery-coil ignition.

No battery, no ignition switch supply and no separate charging circuit are needed for the spark. That is why magnetos are common on small petrol engines such as chainsaws, lawn mowers and some motorcycles, and on aircraft piston engines. The spark energy comes from mechanical rotation, so a magneto must be turned fast enough to make a good spark. At very low cranking speed the output can be weak; an impulse coupling or a separate starting vibrator may be added on some engines.
The distributor, where fitted, sends the high voltage to each plug in turn. A single-cylinder engine can use the same coil and breaker without a distributor.
Battery-coil and magneto systems both use an induction coil and a breaker, but they suit different duties.

blocks.text: A flat battery stops a battery-coil engine. A magneto engine can be hand-started without one. On cars, battery-coil ignition dominated before electronic systems because the battery is already present for starting, lighting and charging.

sections.h3: Dwell: why the spark weakens at high speed

blocks.text: The primary current does not jump to its full value when the points close. The coil's inductance makes it rise along a curve, i = (V ÷ R)(1 − e−t/τ), with time constant τ = L ÷ R. The time the points stay closed is set by the dwell angle, the cam angle for which they are shut. Dwell is a fixed angle, so the time falls as speed rises; at high speed the current is cut before it reaches V ÷ R, the stored energy ½LI² falls, and the spark is weaker. This is the battery-coil system's main limit, and electronic systems fix it by controlling dwell time (see Electronic ignition and laser ignition).

tdwell = dwell angle ÷ (6 × distributor rpm)
tdwell in s; angle in degrees of distributor-cam rotation.

examples.question: A coil has primary inductance L = 6 mH and current I = 4 A at the instant the contact breaker opens. Find the energy stored in the primary magnetic field.
examples.answer: The stored energy is 0.048 J, or 48 mJ.
examples.check:
L = 6e-3
I = 4.0
E = 0.5 * L * I**2
print(E)
print(E * 1000)

examples.question: The coil of the first example (L = 6 mH) has primary resistance 3 Ω on a 12 V supply. A four-cylinder four-stroke engine's distributor cam has 4 lobes and a dwell of 54° per cylinder. Find the dwell time, the primary current at break and the stored energy at 3000 and at 6000 rpm.
steps: Full current V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 A; τ = L ÷ R = 0.006 ÷ 3 = 2 ms.
At 3000 rpm the distributor turns at 1500 rpm: t<sub>dwell</sub> = 54 ÷ (6 × 1500) = 0.006 s = 6 ms.
examples.answer: 6 ms, 3.80 A and 43.3 mJ at 3000 rpm; 3 ms, 3.11 A and 29.0 mJ at 6000 rpm. Doubling the speed cuts the spark energy by a third.

traps: Do not say a magneto needs a battery. A magneto makes its own primary current from a rotating magnet.
Primary current, about 4 A, is not the spark current. The secondary sends a short high-voltage pulse at low current.
The contact breaker interrupts the primary circuit, not the secondary. The secondary voltage appears because the primary field collapses.
A distributor does not make the spark. It routes the coil's high voltage to the correct plug.
The condenser is not only a radio filter. It reduces point arcing and helps the primary current fall fast.

quiz.q: Name the main parts of a battery-coil ignition system.
quiz.a: Battery, ignition switch, primary winding, contact breaker, condenser, secondary winding, distributor and spark plugs.

quiz.q: Why is the secondary winding made of many turns of fine wire?
quiz.a: Many turns give a high induced voltage for the same flux change, enough to jump the plug gap. The secondary current is tiny, so fine wire is enough and keeps the coil small, even though its resistance is high.

quiz.q: What does the condenser do across the contact breaker?
quiz.a: It gives the primary current a path as the points open, reduces arcing, helps the magnetic field collapse quickly and protects the points.

quiz.q: A primary coil has L = 8 mH and current I = 3 A at the instant the breaker opens. Find the stored energy.
Why can a magneto engine start without a battery but a battery-coil engine cannot?
quiz.a: A magneto induces its own primary current from a rotating permanent magnet. A battery-coil system needs the battery to build primary current. Without a battery there is no primary current, so no collapsing field and no secondary spark.

quiz.q: A car with battery-coil ignition cranks but does not fire. The battery is good. List two ignition-side checks and say what each proves.
quiz.a: Check for a spark at a plug or high-tension lead: this tests the coil secondary, distributor and lead. Check primary current and breaker opening: this tests the supply, switch, primary winding and points.

quiz.q: A four-cylinder four-stroke engine with a 4-lobe cam and 50° dwell runs at 4000 rpm. Find the dwell time.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern cars use coil-on-plug ignition with the driver transistor inside each coil, and small engines use capacitor discharge ignition. Aircraft piston engines keep dual magnetos so the engine does not depend on the battery. Search next for ignition coil saturation and inductive versus capacitor discharge ignition.
